newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo government vows clamp down on "grey economy".
newsitem.headline: Yugo government vows clamp down on "grey economy".

text.p: The Yugoslav government has vowed to clamp down on the booming "grey economy" that helped thousands survive through years of economic recession caused by wars, international sanctions and mismanagement.

"Yugoslav borders will be 'hermetically closed' to illegal imports and the federal and republican governments, federal customs, police, Yugoslav army and inspections will work together on this," Yugoslav Trade Minister Milorad Miskovic was quoted as saying by Belgrade media on Wednesday.
Miskovic said the government would tackle the roots of the illegal trade which has gained such proportions it seriously threatens the legal economy and financing of public spending.
Goods will enter the country only after all obligations to the state are met, from turnover and other taxes, to excise and customs duties, with most duties paid at borders, he said.

Since "grey economy" transactions are outside the banking system, in direct cash exchanges or compensation deals, the government proposed the National Bank of Yugoslavia reduce the amount of cash in circulation from the present 45 percent to not more than 25 percent.

It promised tough punishment for fiscal indiscipline ahead of regulations to deny competent state institutions and ministries the right to approve various export-import permits and concessions for individual firms.
Cheaper black market goods have in the last five years bankrupt many large trading companies in an economy strapped by lack of cash and huge internal debts.
Idle industry, operating at just 40 percent of its capacity before the breakup of former Yugoslavia in 1991, left many workers on "compulsory leave", receiving minimum wages.
Hundreds of thousands of people turned to smuggling to survive, peddling black market consumer goods from Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Albania, Italy and other states.

Despite the often dubious quality of goods, many of Belgrade's 2.5 million people, or nearly a fourth of the country's total population, relied heavily on these markets, the biggest of which was recently shut down.
Although it has frequently pledged to do so, the government has done little so far to curb the grey economy, unofficially estimated to account for 40 percent of gross domestic product.

The latest tough stand surprised some analysts who said such unpopular measures in an election year would not raise the ruling Socialist Party's popularity among the poor segments of society struggling to make ends meet.

The clampdown would avoid the "big fry" since many officials have a "cut" in the lucrative businesses, like cigarettes and petrol, which account for the largest part of grey economy, the analysts said.
Health, pension and education funds are empty and strikes of school teachers, doctors, nurses and social workers over late wages have become commonplace.

According to the Federal Statistics Office, the average wage in Yugoslavia in April stood at 733 dinars ($130) while a monthly consumer basket of basic food and drink items for a family of four cost around 1,500, or twice as much.

In May, month-on-month inflation was officially 0.2 percent and year-on-year 21.3 percent, but economic analysts attributed slow price growth also to declining demand amid the population's low purchasing power.

"And they have the nerve to tell us on TV how our living standard is improving, and how we will have double digit growth this year which most western European nations will not," said Nada, a disgruntled 73-year-old pensioner.

Once members of a middle class that has practically disappeared during the past few years, she and her husband had to sell paintings, jewellery, clothes and anything else from their flat to be able to pay bills and expensive medicines.
"If it weren't for the flea market, I don't know what we would have done. I can't afford the prices in shops, so where will I go now?" Nada asked. -- Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
($ = 5.640 dinars)
